declaration.intent: Define what each of the five Forge Stack tools is and how it is actually used, as a factual reference for anyone or anything (including an AI editing assistant) writing or updating documentation about them. This capsule describes behaviour, not house style — pair it with forge-stack/docs/documentation-style-v1 for how to write about these tools, and with giblets-forge/style/readme-style-v1 for README structure.

parameters.authority_note: If a tool's actual CLI flags or behaviour have changed since this capsule was signed, the running code is correct and this capsule is stale — check the tool's own --help output and its implementation-definition doc (where one exists) before trusting this capsule for anything operational.

scp.system_vs_artefact: SCP is the protocol (system). sc is the artefact it produces — always lowercase, always .sc.json.
scp.what_it_is: A declarative protocol for stating intent, parameters, and constraints in a signed, versioned, inheritable document. Every other stage of the stack — DataCube, Leighton Weight, ChronoSCRIBE, HAL — is bound and governed through sc capsules.
scp.what_it_produces: sc — a JSON document with root fields scp_id, scp_version, created, inherits, declaration, licence, signature. A content revision bumps the -vN suffix on scp_id, which creates a new identity, never a mutation of the old one.
how_used: Author a capsule by hand or by copying an existing one as a template, editing declaration.intent and declaration.parameters.
Leave document_sha256 as the literal placeholder COMPUTE-ON-FREEZE if the capsule references an external document.
Run freeze.py to compute and fill any COMPUTE-ON-FREEZE placeholders from the referenced document's actual bytes.
Run sign.py to sign the capsule (and, where it references a non-JSON document via the document field, sign that document too as a detached .sig sidecar).
Run sign.py --verify to confirm the capsule and any referenced artefacts verify.
Pin it: run ledger.py append-pins (optionally --scope <consumer>) to witness the capsule and its document into the appropriate ledger.
scp.tooling: freeze.py, sign.py — no dedicated scp.py; SCP is the substrate every other tool sits on, not a separately invoked tool.
rules_that_matter: A capsule's inherits field records which governance was in force at signing — it is never updated later to point at newer governance.
SCP Lite is a signed minimal subset (scp_id, scp_version, created, declaration, signature only — no inherits or licence) for lightweight bindings.
"Capsule" is prose-only. Never write .scp.json, never call it a capsule in code, a schema field, or a filename.

datacube.system_vs_artefact: DataCube is the system (camel case). cube is the artefact it produces (lowercase).
datacube.what_it_is: The Classify stage. Scores knowledge about a subject across six lenses — FACT, COUNTER, OPINION, FICTION, CONTEXT, UNKNOWN — which are bins, not scores. An empty COUNTER lens means disconfirmation was not sought, not that no counterevidence exists.
datacube.what_it_produces: cube — a signed, deterministic snapshot of everything currently known and classified about a subject, computed from an append-only store rather than hand-edited.
how_used: Write observations into the store: python datacube.py write (or equivalent store-write command) — records go under namespaces event.*, state.*, domain.*, behaviour.*, independent of which lens they're classified into.
Verify the store: python datacube.py verify-store — checks the append-only chain hasn't been tampered with.
Project a cube: python datacube.py project (or score/classify) — deterministically computes the current cube from the store; running this twice on the same store state produces a byte-identical cube.
Sign and pin: sign.py signs the cube, ledger.py append-pins witnesses it plus a store checkpoint event.
rules_that_matter: DataCube keeps a store. The word "ledger" is reserved for ChronoSCRIBE — never call DataCube's store a ledger.

The integrity denominator (how "complete" a cube's classification is judged to be) is currently a configurable saturation model, not yet a governance-ratified formula — treat any integrity percentage as provisional.
A cube is a snapshot at a point in the store's history, not a live view — re-project it after new observations land if you need the current picture.

leighton_weight_engine.system_vs_artefact: Leighton Weight Engine is the system/stage. Leighton Weight (λ) is the artefact/value it produces — a trust score, 0.00–2.00.
leighton_weight_engine.what_it_is: The Trust-score stage. Computes how much an entity's word is currently worth, based on an observation stream of attestations about that entity's past claims and actions.
leighton_weight_engine.what_it_produces: λ — never stored, always computed fresh from the observation stream at an explicit as_of time using the neutral-attractor decay curve: λ(t) = 1.00 + (λ0 − 1.00) × e^(−kt). Decay pulls toward neutral (1.00), not toward zero — an entity that goes quiet drifts toward "unknown", not "distrusted".
how_used: Record an observation/attestation into the entity's observation stream (event.attestation.issued via ledger.py attest, or a direct store write depending on context).
Score an entity: python leighton_weight.py score --k-per-day <value> — --k-per-day is mandatory, there is no default, because k must always be calibrated per domain and the tool refuses to guess.
Verify a score: python leighton_weight.py verify-score.

Run the worked example end-to-end: python leighton_weight.py worked-example --output-dir <dir> --k-per-day <value> — useful for confirming the pipeline (write, verify-store, score, verify-score, determinism check) is healthy before scoring something real.
Pin a score: ledger.py append-pins witnesses the score and a store checkpoint.
rules_that_matter: k is the decay constant. It is never called λ. It is always per-domain — the value used in worked examples is a demonstration constant, not a calibrated production value.

Disputes over an attestation are resolved using the disputing party's λ as it stood strictly before the attestation was made, never their current λ — this stops winning a dispute from retroactively inflating the standing that won it.
The outcome-to-λ-delta mapping (how much a given observed outcome moves the score) is currently hardcoded in the tool, not yet ratified as governance policy.

chronoscribe.full_name: Signed Chronological Record of Immutable Behavioural Events
chronoscribe.system_vs_artefact: ChronoSCRIBE is the system. ledger is the artefact — never shortened to "Chrono" or "Scribe" in formal documentation.
chronoscribe.what_it_is: The Audit stage. A hash-chained, append-only, signed record of events. Every other stage's outputs get witnessed here — document pins, capsule pins, cube materialisations, scores, seals.
chronoscribe.what_it_produces: ledger.jsonl — one JSON line per event, each entry's prev field carrying the hash of the previous line, each entry individually Ed25519-signed.
how_used: First-ever creation of a ledger: python genesis.py — mints the first immutable batch. genesis.py refuses to run if a ledger already exists at that path; it is genesis-only, never an append tool.

All subsequent additions: python ledger.py append-pins (optionally --scope <consumer>) — scans capsules/documents for anything not yet pinned and witnesses them; refuses to append anything with an unresolved placeholder hash (e.g. literal COMPUTE-ON-FREEZE).
A single custom event: python ledger.py append --event <name> --subject <id> --sha256 <hash>.
Record an attestation: python ledger.py attest --subject-hash <hash> --outcome <value> [--rationale <text>].
Verify: python ledger.py verify (optionally --scope <consumer>) — walks the full chain and every signature; use --dry-run on append-pins to preview before writing.

A new consumer's first ledger entry is event.ledger.anchor.root, which pins the root ledger's current head hash so the consumer chain is provably rooted in a specific state of the constitution, not just asserted to be related to it.
chronoscribe.tooling: genesis.py (root ledger creation only), ledger.py (everything after: verify, append, append-pins, attest)
rules_that_matter: The root ledger records the constitution only. Consumer-specific capsules belong in that consumer's own ledger, created via --scope, not the root.

Unpublished, local-only ledger rows may be safely discarded if something goes wrong. Once a ledger has been pushed/published, its rows are permanent — never delete a published entry, even to fix an error; append a correcting entry instead.
A capsule pin records scp_id + sha256, not a file path — moving a capsule's file location does not invalidate its existing pins.

hal.system_vs_artefact: HAL is the system. seal is the artefact it produces.
hal.what_it_is: The Act stage. The gate through which any consequential action must pass a named human authoriser, whose standing (λ) is checked against a tier requirement before the action is permitted.
hal.what_it_produces: seal — a signed record of an authorisation decision, including the authoriser's identity, their λ at the time, the tier requested, and — critically — refusals as well as approvals.
how_used: Seal a decision: python hal.py seal --authoriser-score-file <path> --tier <n> [other action-specific args] — the authoriser's λ is read from a verified score file (produced by leighton_weight.py score), never entered manually; the command refuses to seal if that λ is insufficient for the requested tier.
Verify a seal: python hal.py verify-seal.
Pin a seal: python hal.py pin-seal (or via ledger.py append-pins, depending on current wiring) — witnesses the seal into the ledger.
rules_that_matter: Every seal carries a separation field: none means the authoriser's score file was signed by the same key as the seal itself; verified means a distinct identity issued the score. Right now this project runs single-operator, so every seal currently reads none — that is stated honestly in the seal itself, not hidden.

A single-operator seal records deliberation and intent. It does not yet prove independence, because there isn't any yet — don't describe single-operator seals as providing the separation-of-concerns guarantee the tier system is ultimately designed to give.

Tiers 1–5 map to λ thresholds, with quarantine below 0.60. Which real-world consequence class sits on which tier is defined by the consumer, not by HAL itself — HAL provides the ladder, not the mapping.
HAL currently has no multi-validator flow and no answer for what a Tier 5 quorum means with more than one signer — this is blocked on having a second real operator, not on more code.
